How each question is handled

Group living standards

  • Starts from the year 1 cash change for each group, from the static analysis.
  • Each later year is compared with the static estimate held flat, so the chart shows what the employment and growth effects add.
  • The employment effect adds people moving into work, net of tax and Universal Credit withdrawal, without double counting anything in the year 1 estimate.
  • The growth effect takes the extra GDP from new workers, converts it to the chosen measure of living standards, removes their own wages, shares the rest equally across the UK population and gives the group its per-person share.

Poverty

  • Starts from the package's own year 1 poverty estimate.
  • Each later year is compared with the package estimate held flat. Under ‘Cohort keeps reform’ the effects are scaled to a group the size of the starting group.
  • The employment effect adds the remaining moves into work, phased in. The share of entrants who leave poverty is measured in Understanding Society households (74% on entering work, about 85% after two years), so in-work poverty is allowed for.
  • Growth is excluded from relative poverty, which it leaves unchanged.

Moves into work follow the timing observed in Understanding Society for 18 to 23-year-olds out of work: 33% of the five-year effect in year 1, 52% by year 2, 73% by year 3, 91% by year 4. Illustrative estimates rather than a full microsimulation.

Technical write-up

Beyond the morning after: how long-term effects change who wins and loses from policy reform

The United Kingdom has experienced fifteen years of weak productivity growth and stagnant wages, yet many reforms that economists agree would raise growth remain unenacted1, partly because the analysis that frames debate is static, recording who loses from a reform on the day it takes effect while saying nothing about the gains that follow as people move into work and the economy grows. Reforms whose costs are immediate and concentrated, and whose benefits are delayed and widely shared, are therefore judged on their costs alone.

This bias bears on two kinds of policy in particular, reforms with short-term losers but long-term winners, and reforms intended to raise growth, which almost always create some losers at the outset. Dynamic models that capture the later gains do exist, but they are laborious, usually applied by academics years after a policy has been enacted and confined to a handful of questions. Policy makers are left with static analysis that is usable but incomplete, and dynamic analysis that is unusable when decisions are made.

This note sets out a model GGF has built to close that gap. It takes the static estimate of a reform as given and adds an employment effect and a growth effect year by year, drawing on new analysis of Understanding Society (USOC) and the Office for Budget Responsibility’s own conventions, and we test it against the academic evidence using an illustrative reform of support for young people with health conditions.

We apply this model to a hypothetical welfare reform, that leaves some young people worse off, thereby increasing poverty, but from which half enter work. We find that by adding these long-run gain from work effects and the impact of the growth this additional work generates we can fundamentally change the interpretation of the effect of the policy, turning something that makes the group affected worse off in year 0 better off over time.

Key findings:

  • Static analysis misses most of the story for reforms that move people into work: in our illustrative reform, a static loss of £3.0bn a year for 1 million young people becomes a gain to the group from year 11 once moves into work are counted.
  • A rise in poverty of 50,000 eventually becomes a fall of around 31,000: because 74% of young people in poverty leave it on entering work, the increase shown by the static estimate is reversed within two years, and on an absolute measure, which also captures the gains from growth, poverty is around 41,000 lower by year ten.
  • The growth effect is real, and how much reaches the group depends on the fiscal stance: with new cohorts joining the reform, around 1 million extra young people are in work by year ten, adding around £57bn a year to GDP and around £27bn a year to the public finances, and when this Exchequer gain is returned to everyone equally, our central case, around £0.5bn a year of it reaches a group of 1 million affected.
  • Wages can fall as employment rises: an influx of young low-skilled workers on this scale could lower similar workers’ wages by around 7% by year ten, a cost that static analysis and simple dynamic scoring both miss.

1. Why static analysis holds back growth

Static distributional analysis calculates the change in each household’s income from a reform with employment, hours and wages held fixed, describing incomes on the morning after a reform rather than once people have responded. Official estimates of growth effects are produced separately by the OBR and usually only if the policy is part of the annual budget and is above a threshold of 0.1% of potential output2. Few are never traced back to the households that bear the first-round losses.

As an example, the Mirrlees Review recommended abolishing stamp duty land tax and other inefficient taxes in 2011, warning that although some changes would be politically difficult, failure to reform imposes enduring costs3. Few today have been enacted, which is naturally a consequence of political factors, but we argue is compounded by the methodological limitations of the way in which each reform would be assessed in public debate.

Without a practical way of showing those gains alongside the losses, the case for growth is always argued at a disadvantage.

Key term: dynamic scoring

Dynamic scoring adds the behavioural and economic responses to a policy into the assessment of its effects. Static analysis assumes nobody changes what they do, whereas dynamic scoring allows for people moving into work, firms investing and the economy growing as a result. It is routine for major tax changes in the United States, but the models involved are slow and specialist, which is why they are rarely used when UK policy is being decided.

2. What the model does

2.1 Starting from the static estimate

Our model takes a package’s own static results as given, including the number affected, their average cash change or decile breakdown and the immediate change in poverty, so every projection matches the official figure at the start. The user also sets how the reform is held over time and whether the static estimate already counts some movement into work.

2.2 The employment effect, built on Understanding Society

Projecting what happens after someone moves into work needs data that follow the same people for many years. We link eleven waves of Understanding Society from 2009-10 to 2023-24, around 466,000 person-year records, and follow everyone who moved into work to measure their pay and whether their household left poverty4. Each new worker follows the measured pay path for their age, net of tax and the Universal Credit taper. The gradual build-up in Table 1 matches the international evidence, with a review of more than 200 evaluations of employment programmes finding effects close to zero at first and growing over two to three years5, and the UK’s Future Jobs Fund leaving young people around 11 percentage points more likely to be in work two years later6. US evidence shows the response is concentrated among people with less severe conditions7, so the model applies it only to those whose health permits work. Chart 1 shows how much faster pay rises for those who enter work young.

2.3 The growth effect, applying OBR principles to a subgroup

Turning extra employment into a growth effect that can be attributed to the people affected raises five questions, which the OBR answers for the economy as a whole but which have not previously been answered for a specific group of households. The model handles each in turn, and in every case it follows the spirit of OBR conventions where they exist and calibrates to the OBR’s aggregate results where they do not.

Does output rise with employment?

A key OBR assumption is that firms invest to equip new workers, so that capital per worker is unchanged and output rises in proportion to the number employed. If capital did not respond, each new worker would add less, and with labour receiving around 60% of national income the short-run growth effect would be around 40% smaller. The model adopts the OBR assumption and extends it beyond the OBR’s five-year forecast horizon, since the reforms it is designed to assess play out over a decade or more.

How productive are new workers?

The OBR assumes that people returning from health-related inactivity are around two-thirds as productive as the average worker8, a figure that reflects the earnings of a typical adult who left work through ill health. Young entrants earn around 40% of average pay, so applying the same ratio to them would credit each with output of around three times their pay, and would imply more extra GDP per job than the OBR’s own judgement that measures raising employment by 0.3% add around 0.2% to GDP because new joiners work fewer hours and earn less than average9.

The model handles this challenge by starting each new worker at half of average output per worker, around £38,000 a year, and lets this rise in line with their measured pay as they gain experience, so that a young entrant whose pay grows quickly also becomes more productive over time. We chose this starting point because it reproduces the relationship between employment and output that the OBR uses at the level of the whole economy. In its March 2023 forecast, the OBR estimated that the labour market measures announced that spring would raise employment by around 0.3% and GDP by around 0.2%, because many of the new workers would work fewer hours and earn less than average, which implies that each 1% rise in employment adds around 0.67% to GDP. Applied to our illustrative reform, the half-of-average assumption produces a very similar figure, with around 1 million extra workers by year ten, as new cohorts join the reform, raising employment by around 3% and GDP by around 2%, or around 0.65% more GDP for each 1% more employment. Because the OBR’s figures are rounded, this should be read as matching the OBR’s judgement in broad terms rather than to the decimal point.

Had we instead applied the OBR’s two-thirds assumption to young entrants, the same workers would have added around £76bn a year to GDP by year ten, or around 0.9% more GDP for each 1% more employment, while assuming they were as productive as the average worker would have added around £86bn. Both figures would sit well above the OBR’s own judgement for how much output a worker produces relative to their pay. Across the economy labour receives around 60% of output, so the average worker produces around 1.7 times what they are paid, whereas we find young entrants in Understanding Society earn around £15,300 a year, which means even our assumption credits them with output of around 2.5 times their pay. The two-thirds assumption would raise this to around 3.3 times their pay and the average worker assumption to around five times, implying that young people entering work for the first time would be two to three times more productive relative to their pay than the typical worker, both of which are at odds with international studies that show productivity broadly tracks pay.

Studies linking firms’ output to their workers’ ages find that young workers’ pay is closely associated with what they produce10, which is why our alternative is matched to pay identified in USOC data and from which the resulting output is calibrated to OBR ratios of pay to output.

How much of extra output reaches households?

Not every pound of GDP becomes household income, since part goes to depreciation, overseas investors and retained profits. The model therefore converts extra output into household disposable income by default, which is around 60% of GDP and is the measure closest to the real incomes used in distributional analysis, since it captures what households actually have to spend after tax and benefits.

The two broader measures each answer a different and useful question. Net national income, around 87% of GDP, measures the income that accrues to UK residents once depreciation and overseas flows are accounted for, including the extra tax revenue and company profits that a reform generates, so it shows the gain to the nation as a whole and the resources available to government and firms to reinvest or redistribute. GDP per person counts every pound of extra output and is the measure used by the OBR and in most international comparisons, so it shows the full scale of what a reform adds to the economy and allows the results to be set directly against official forecasts.

The model then deducts the new workers’ own gross pay, because their earnings are already counted in the employment effect and would otherwise be counted twice.

Who receives the growth, and what happens to the Exchequer gain?

Extra employment also improves the public finances, since new workers pay tax and claim less in benefits and the wider output they generate is taxed, a gain of around £27bn a year by year ten in our illustrative reform. What happens to this Exchequer gain is a decision for government rather than an economic effect, so the model offers three options. Our central case assumes the gain is returned to everyone equally, for example through lower taxes or higher spending, so the group receives its per person share of around £0.5bn a year by year ten for a group of 1 million. This is a fairly standard assumption when testing the macroeconomic effect of policy reforms, such that the full effect is isolated to the reform itself and not reflective of current economic conditions.

If the Exchequer instead retains the gain to reduce borrowing, households receive only their after-tax share of the extra output and the group gains around £0.1bn, whereas if the gain from the new workers themselves is recycled to the group affected, the group gains around £7bn a year and is better off within two years. While the latter is generous, it is reasonable as a scenario as government may whish to compensate a group that has lost out with the induced tax revenues. In the Autumn Budget 2021, weeks after ending the £20-a-week pandemic uplift to Universal Credit, the government cut the Universal Credit taper rate from 63% to 55% and raised work allowances by £500 a year, worth around £2.2bn a year to around two million low-paid families11.

How does growth affect poverty?

Growth raises incomes across the population, including at the median, so it leaves relative poverty unchanged while reducing absolute poverty, which is measured against a line fixed in real terms. The model therefore applies the growth effect to absolute poverty only, and attributes all of the change in relative poverty to people moving into work.

3. An illustrative reform

To show the model at work, we apply it to a stylised reform that initially affects 1 million people aged 16 to 23 with health conditions, with an average static loss of £3,000 a year and an immediate rise in poverty of 50,000. The reform applies to each new cohort as it reaches 16, so around 125,000 more young people join it each year, and we assume that 45% of those affected move into work at some point, 450,000 of the starting group and around 1 million in total by year ten, with the first year of that response already in the static estimate. Results for the group are shown for a group the size of the starting million, and all of these are placeholder values rather than estimates of any announced package.

Chart 2 shows that the static estimate substantially overstates the long-run cost to the group. The employment effect cuts the £3.0bn loss to around £0.9bn by year five and £0.5bn by year ten, recovering more than four-fifths of it, in line with the Netherlands, where people replaced around 62 cents of every euro of disability benefit lost through higher earnings12. Growth then tips the group into gain from year eleven, because extra GDP reaches around £57bn a year by year ten, around 2% of GDP, and when the Exchequer gain is returned to everyone equally around £0.5bn a year of it reaches the group, enough to close the gap that the employment effect leaves.

The poverty results are where the dynamic picture differs most from the static one. The static estimate shows 50,000 more young people in poverty, but around 28% of those out of work are in household poverty and 74% of them leave it on entering work, so as moves into work build up the rise is reversed by year two, and relative poverty settles at around 31,000 below what it would have been without the reform from year four onwards, a swing of around 81,000 against the static estimate. Chart 3 shows how this compares across the two measures of poverty that the model reports.

The two measures diverge because they treat growth differently. Relative poverty counts people living below 60% of the median income in the same year, so when growth raises incomes across the population it lifts the median, and the poverty line with it, by as much as it lifts the incomes of people near the line, which leaves the number in relative poverty unchanged once the employment response is complete. Absolute poverty instead measures incomes against a line held fixed in real terms, so every rise in incomes from growth carries some people over it, and absolute poverty keeps falling after the employment response has finished, to around 41,000 below the no-reform level by year ten and around 46,000 by year fifteen. The gap between the two lines is therefore the contribution of growth to poverty reduction, which a relative measure on its own will always miss.

The evidence also points to what the model leaves out, since studies that link microsimulation to a model of the whole economy show that reforms which raise labour supply can lift employment while lowering wages13. Using standard estimates of how easily workers of different ages and qualifications substitute for one another14, the around 1 million extra young low-skilled workers in work by year ten could lower similar workers’ wages by around 7%, costing those already in work around £3.3bn a year, far more than the group gains from growth. Against this, the model does not count the lasting pay penalty that youth unemployment leaves, estimated at 13 to 21 per cent by age 4215, which earlier entry to work partly avoids.

These estimates are illustrative rather than a forecast or a full cost-benefit analysis. The results depend most on the share of people who move into work, the productivity of new workers and whether wages adjust, and pay growth is measured only for people who stay in work, so it is likely to be overstated. The value of the model is that it makes these assumptions visible and shows the gains from reform alongside the losses when a decision is made, which is the evidence a growth strategy needs and does not currently have.
